articles.title: Cannabis hospitalisations up 49% in a decade, new study shows
articles.author: Myfanwy Graham, NHMRC Postgraduate Scholar and Fulbright Alumna in Public Health Policy, Monash University
articles.summary: More people are ending up in hospital after using cannabis than a decade ago, and psychosis rates are rising. Here’s what can explain the rise.
articles.contentHtml:
Doctors have raised growing concerns about rising rates of cannabis-related psychosis.

Our new ten-year study shows those concerns are well founded.

We looked at almost 40,000 cannabis-related hospital admissions in Victoria between 2013 and 2023. Over that time, cases where cannabis was the main reason someone ended up in hospital increased by 49%.

Psychotic disorder (commonly called psychosis) was the leading cause.

What we did and what we found

We examined hospital records for 39,565 cannabis-related hospital admissions in Victoria over the ten-year period.

Admissions peaked during the COVID pandemic in 2020 and 2021. Cannabis-related psychosis was the main driver across the decade, accounting for 40.1% of hospitalisations where cannabis was the main reason. Poisoning made up less than 12% of cases.

These weren’t quick visits. Most patients (68%) stayed in hospital for longer than 24 hours, with the average stay lasting a week for all cases involving cannabis. This suggests these cases were serious. More than 1,500 people required admission to an intensive care unit (ICU).

Males aged 15–24 still represent the largest total group hospitalised. But our study showed the largest increase over the decade was in younger women and adults aged 65 and older.

Read more: Cannabis isn’t ‘safer’ in your 20s and 30s – it’s linked to an earlier onset of psychosis

What can explain the findings?

During 2020 and 2021, isolation, job losses and broader mental health struggles may have contributed to many people using more cannabis.

Wastewater monitoring confirmed a rise in cannabis use around this time. Unlike some illicit supply chains disrupted by border closures, local cannabis supply remained largely accessible.

Demographics in cannabis use are shifting too. The proportion of people who have ever used cannabis has risen over the decade. More women are also using cannabis in high-risk ways, including frequent use, which may increase the risk of cannabis dependence.

Changing social perceptions may play a role. As cannabis becomes more acceptable, people may simply feel more comfortable telling doctors about their cannabis use.

Higher-strength cannabis is also likely to play role. We are seeing severe psychiatric and respiratory reactions with products containing higher levels of tetrahydrocannabinol (or THC). That’s the component that can cause drowsiness or a high.

Is medicinal cannabis to blame?

It is hard to know if prescribed medicinal cannabis or illicit cannabis explains this increase in hospitalisations. Hospital coding systems – used in health records and in the data we examined – rarely distinguish between legal (prescribed) and illicit cannabis use; many people use both.

Fewer Australians take prescribed compared to illicit cannabis. Even then, legal products come with risks.

Higher-potency products that can be inhaled are generally not recommended for safety reasons. But these are some of the most frequently prescribed products, with some containing up to 88% THC.

High-volume telehealth clinics that don’t properly screen people for existing mental health conditions or other risk factors before prescribing high-strength cannabis may also be contributing to the rise in severe mental health adverse events.

Without proper clinical monitoring, risks may not be detected, or will be detected later, and harms may be more severe by the time problems are identified.

Read more: Medicinal cannabis has gone mainstream. But Australia’s struggling to cope

There are wider issues

This isn’t just a Victorian issue. In fact, some studies suggest other states have higher rates of cannabis use.

Nationally, cannabis remains one of the top illicit drugs leading to a hospital admission, outpacing illicit opioids.

International data shows a similar trend. When legal access expands via profit-driven commercial models, cannabis-related psychosis hospitalisations tend to rise.

Our findings that the largest increase in cannabis-related hospitalisations was in younger women and older adults has wider implications.

Public health initiatives don’t necessarily focus on these groups. By identifying who is most vulnerable, we have an opportunity to tailor prevention campaigns, improve clinical screening before cannabis is prescribed and more broadly for vulnerable groups, and ensure safety regulations keep pace with changing products and increased availability.

Myfanwy Graham receives funding from the Australian National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC). She has received state government and Department of Health, Disability and Ageing funding for independent reviews on medicinal cannabis. She has served as a consultant for the UNODC, WHO and NASEM, and is an appointed member of the Therapeutic Goods Administration's Medicinal Cannabis Expert Working Group. This article does not represent the views of the TGA or the Expert Working Group.

Suzanne Nielsen receives funding from the competitive research schemes (NHMRC, MMRF) and philanthropy. She is the current president of the Australasian Professional Society on Alcohol and other Drugs (APSAD). She has previously completed independent evidence reviews on medicinal cannabis for the TGA and Worksafe.

articles.title: ‘Lazy, weak, bewitched’ – how stigma stops Uganda’s children from getting help, and what schools can do about it
articles.author: Lydia Namatende-Sakwa, Associate Research Scientist, African Population and Health Research Center
articles.summary: School mental health programmes must address both emotional wellbeing and structural pressures such as poverty, stigma and exclusion.
articles.contentHtml:
“Me who is a poor person, do I have the luxury to have depression? No, it is only you who is rich that has the luxury to have depression.”

This statement, shared by a research participant in Kampala, the Ugandan capital, captures a persistent misconception: that depression belongs to wealthy people or those whose lives are comfortable enough to permit emotional vulnerability.

It is an example of how socio-cultural beliefs can become a barrier to recognising mental health problems and seeking support.

In 2025, Uganda’s Ministry of Education and Sports issued a set of mental health and psychosocial support policy guidelines and resources for schools. These included a training manual, teachers’ handbook and wellbeing guide. They provide practical information on recognising distress, psychosocial support, referral and wellbeing in education settings.

The next challenge is to put the guidelines into practice.

Our team of researchers at the African Health and Population Research Center did a study to provide evidence that would help schools in Uganda follow the guidelines. We looked at what people understand by mental health, what learners and staff need, school capacity and what needs to happen first to put the guidelines into action.

The study engaged 200 learners, teachers, parents, community representatives, policy actors and development partners across four districts: Kampala, Jinja, Gulu and Mbarara. Kampala is the capital city; Jinja is a mixed rural-urban context. Gulu is an area affected by conflict and displacement. Mbarara is an education and economic hub with urban and rural schools.

We found socio-cultural and gender norms strongly influenced whose distress was recognised, how it was explained and whether seeking help was considered acceptable. Mental health at school was linked to issues like literacy, spirituality, poverty, family instability, displacement, disability and trauma.

Learner distress reflected overlapping academic, family, economic, social and institutional pressures. The responses at school must take all these into account. School mental health programmes must address both emotional wellbeing and structural pressures such as poverty, stigma and exclusion.

Listening to Ugandans

Our four study sites were chosen to reflect a range of environments, with different resources and socio-cultural influences.

We held dialogues at each site with learners aged 13-18, parents, teachers, government representatives, youth-led organisations, religious and community leaders, NGOs and researchers. Special interest groups (including refugees, LGBTQ organisations and people with disabilities) were also included.

The dialogues explored understandings of mental health, learner and staff needs, school capacity and future priorities.

What’s influencing mental health

The study participants described student mental health as a growing concern. They mentioned depression, anxiety, stress, low self-esteem, fear, social withdrawal, substance use, bullying-related distress, trauma, anger, academic pressure and poor emotional regulation.

Participants described these as interconnected problems.

The drivers of distress among students were identified as:

  • academic pressure

  • family and home background, including absent parents, domestic violence and neglect

  • poverty that resulted in lower self-esteem and greater exclusion from peer groups

  • bullying, teasing, humiliation and harsh discipline

  • substance use and addiction, especially among boys and urban learners.

Boys and girls were seen as vulnerable to different pressures.

Barriers to getting help

Participants in all sites said mental illness carried a stigma. It was seen as morally wrong, caused by supernatural forces, or “a disease for the rich”.

Another perception was that boys and men couldn’t seek help for fear of looking weak.

Learners also felt they could not trust adults with their problems. They feared that teachers might judge them or reveal their personal stories publicly. Learners experiencing anxiety or distress thought they might be labelled lazy or badly behaved, or accused of “faking it” or “seeking attention”.

The danger is that withdrawal, poor concentration, anger or declining performance might then be treated as deliberate disobedience.

Mental health difficulties were sometimes attributed to witchcraft, curses or demonic possession. Religious and cultural systems can offer hope, belonging and support, but problems arise when they become the only explanation for distress. As one Kampala teacher warned,

Some people will pray until somebody dies.

Learners reported being told, “You have to be strong … a guy who does not cry.” Such expectations encourage boys to hide stress and may lead to withdrawal, anger or risky behaviour rather than seeking support.

Girls face pressures linked to harassment, poverty, reproductive-health stigma and social judgment, often while being expected to remain silent. Female educators also face gendered scrutiny, including questions such as, “Where are their husbands and why are they not interested in staying with them?”

Counselling can itself carry stigma. People reported fear and shame associated with getting professional help.

Changing systems to change norms

Teachers should recognise that a child’s behaviour may arise from bullying, poverty, bereavement or family conflict. Schools should ask not only “What is wrong?” but also “What may have happened?”

School mental health programmes should respect cultural beliefs without delaying appropriate help.

Girls should be protected from harassment and enabled to report problems confidentially. Schools should promote a broader understanding of masculinity in which recognising emotions and seeking help are seen as responsible behaviours.

Schools need private support spaces, clear confidentiality procedures and counselling that is normalised. Learners must be able to seek help before problems escalate.

Socio-cultural and gender norms are reinforced through everyday practices and cannot be changed through awareness messages alone. Uganda’s response must combine norm change with system change. Schools need culturally grounded mental health literacy, safe environments, respectful discipline, confidential support, gender-transformative programming, trained staff and links to health and community services.

The key question is whether schools can recognise distress without judgment and respond with dignity, protection and appropriate care.

Lydia Namatende-Sakwa does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Students from military families are often misunderstood in US public schools – a retired military officer and behavioral health expert explains what schools can do
articles.author: Nikki R Wooten, Associate Professor of Social Work, University of South Carolina
articles.summary: Students from military families have specific experiences and needs that require support from their schools.
articles.contentHtml:
Over 1.4 million children had a parent or caregiver who served in the U.S. armed forces in 2024.

Among active-duty families, 2.4% of military children had both parents serving in the military. Another 4% lived in single-parent households.

More than 90% of these children attend U.S. public schools. Over 67,000 attend Department of Defense schools located in the U.S. and foreign countries. Military-connected students have a unique set of experiences and academic and emotional needs, including support with school transitions and developing a sense of belonging at their new school.

Because only 6% of Americans have served in the U.S. military, some educators may not understand the experiences of military children and the challenges of military life.

As a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel and military behavioral health expert, I think there are a few key ways that school districts can better support these students through school transitions.

Some strategies include identifying military-connected students during enrollment and training educators about military life.

Benefits and drawbacks of military life

The military lifestyle creates both unique opportunities and challenges for children and teenagers whose parents are military service members.

Military children often travel and have opportunities to live in multiple cities across the U.S. and other countries. They are also exposed to different cultures, new traditions and opportunities to learn foreign languages.

These children are resilient and adaptable. They may also display increased independence, personal growth and pride because of their parent’s military service. Many are thriving in school because of these traits.

Military children are also twice as likely to serve in the military as their civilian peers.

But military life can also be stressful for children.

Many children with parents in the military move frequently. They often live in more cities and attend more schools than their civilian peers – an average of two schools during high school, and for most, six to nine different schools between kindergarten and 12th grade.

They experience their parent being away from home for various periods of time, ranging from a few weeks at a time to a year or more.

They also fear that their parent might be hurt or killed while serving in the military.

As a result, military children and teenagers may experience social withdrawal, angry outbursts and mental health problems, including depression and anxiety. These challenges might also cause them to miss school, struggle to complete school assignments and have difficulty making new friends.

Recent research found that military-connected students were more likely to be disengaged in school and repeat a grade than their civilian peers. Other studies found that multiple parental deployments and longer parental separations affected children negatively. Examples include greater family stress and behavioral problems.

A stressful experience

Children’s responses to military life vary, depending on how old they are and their level of maturity. Children 5 and younger often have limited language skills to express their feelings. As a result, they may act out behaviorally in response to changes in caregivers and daily routines.

Elementary school students may have tantrums, be clingy, have toileting accidents, engage in uncontrollable crying or become less talkative as a result of changes in schools, homes and caregivers.

Middle school students and preteens, ages 8 to 13, are likely aware of how their lives are different from their civilian peers.

These students may have experienced multiple moves and attended multiple schools over their relatively short lives. They may respond to changes in schools and household routines with angry outbursts, irritability, anxiety and social withdrawal.

They may also have fluctuating grades, peer conflict, problems completing their homework and disciplinary problems at school.

Boys and girls may express their stress differently. Boys may exhibit more anger and aggression, whereas girls might demonstrate sadness, depression and self-harm.

Military adolescents and high school students, typically 14-18, have heightened risk for anxiety, depression and suicide due to military-related stressors, especially during parental deployments.

They may experience mood changes, anger and social withdrawal. They may also disengage from school activities, perform poorly in school and choose to skip classes. Many are also high achievers despite the challenges of military life.

Military adolescents are also at risk for substance use.

My prior research from 2019 found that military adolescents had frequent emergency department visits and hospitalizations for substance use problems during the Afghanistan and Iraq wars.

How schools can support military-connected students

Military-connected students transitioning to a new school often need help early in the process to ensure they have adjusted well to their new school.

As a licensed clinical social worker and former child therapist for military children, I think brief check-ins with a school counselor or social worker are necessary to identify concerns early. These check-ins can help avoid behavioral or academic difficulties and prevent a problem from becoming worse.

U.S. public schools are required to identify students with an active duty military parent, typically by asking about military affiliation during enrollment.

Some school districts also include children of veterans and those with parents in the National Guard and Reserves in these records.

Research has consistently shown that the impact of military life continues after parents leave military service.

An estimated 2.3 million children under 18 reside with a veteran who is disabled. These children often assume caregiving responsibilities for siblings and their veteran parent.

Identifying schools that support military-connected students

State education departments can give schools a Purple Star School designation, indicating that the school is committed to assisting with the academic, social and emotional needs of military-connected students. These schools maintain a list of military students, help students with school transitions and train school personnel about the challenges of military life.

Currently, there are over 4,100 Purple Star Schools in 44 states across the U.S.

The proportion of military-connected students in U.S. public schools depends on the military and veteran population of each state and school district, as well as the geographical location of military installations.

Texas, California, Florida, North Carolina, Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia rank among the 10 states with the most military families that have children attending public schools.

Schools can help military-connected children and their families by creating a welcoming school climate, maintaining open communication with students and parents, and developing student groups and peer-support programs.

Frequent school guidance counselor, nurse or social worker visits may also be needed. High schools can develop peer-mentoring programs and suicide prevention, mental health awareness and anti-stigma campaigns.

I think it is also important for schools not to rush to identify behaviors as a disciplinary problem when family stress is the root cause.

Although military-connected students face unique challenges to success in school, I think schools should intervene early and often to meet their needs. Helping these students ensures every child has an equal chance to succeed in school.

Nikki R. Wooten, PhD, LISW-CP previously received research funding from the National Institute on Drug Abuse. Dr. Wooten retired as a lieutenant colonel from the U. S. Army after over 33 years of military service. The statements wherein are the author's and do not necessarily represent the official position of the U.S. Department of War, U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, or the U.S. Government.

articles.title: Why antidepressants can stop working after initially helping
articles.author: Colin Davidson, Professor of Neuropharmacology, University of Lancashire
articles.summary: Antidepressant tachyphylaxis describes the loss of a treatment response that was once effective. Here’s what scientists know so far.
articles.contentHtml:
Antidepressant use continues to rise. In England, 96 million antidepressant prescription items were dispensed to an estimated 9.1 million patients in 2025 to 2026. These medicines are prescribed for depression and other conditions, including anxiety and some forms of pain.

Antidepressants can take several weeks to work fully, can cause unwanted side-effects and do not help everyone sufficiently. But there is another potential problem: a treatment that initially works can sometimes appear to lose its effect.

This is known as antidepressant tachyphylaxis: someone initially improves while taking an antidepressant, but their symptoms later return or worsen despite continuing the same medicine at the same dose. It has also been called antidepressant “poop-out” or “breakthrough depression”.

Tachyphylaxis describes a different pattern from treatment-resistant depression. While definitions vary, treatment-resistant depression generally means that someone has not improved sufficiently after trying at least two antidepressants, taken at suitable doses for long enough to assess their effect. With tachyphylaxis, the person initially benefited before apparently losing that improvement.

Why might an antidepressant stop helping?

Exactly why this happens is unclear. One possibility is that the brain gradually adapts to prolonged exposure to an antidepressant. These medicines affect chemical messengers that nerve cells use to communicate, including serotonin, which is involved in mood and other functions.

Research suggests that antidepressant treatment can change how cells respond to serotonin. Some of these changes involve receptors: proteins on cells that receive chemical signals. Receptors can become less responsive during treatment, altering communication between nerve cells.

However, this research does not establish why a previously helpful medicine might stop helping. One review of serotonin changes examined experiments in rats, while another explored mechanisms involved in antidepressant action. Neither establishes a proven sequence in which these changes first relieve depression and later cause it to return.

One possibility is that the brain gradually adjusts to the medicine, so the same dose has less effect than before. This is called tolerance, but researchers have not established whether it explains why antidepressants seem to stop helping some people.

There are also other reasons why symptoms may return. Someone may have missed doses, developed another health problem or experienced a worsening of their depression despite treatment. Another medicine could also affect their treatment.

The difficulty is that returning symptoms do not reveal which explanation applies. A recurrence of depression while someone is taking an antidepressant does not, by itself, demonstrate that their body has developed tolerance to it.

How common is it?

This uncertainty makes the problem difficult to measure. A review published in 2019 reported rates of tachyphylaxis ranging from 9% to 57%, depending on who was studied and how long they were followed.

That wide range does not tell us how likely any one person is to experience the problem. The studies used different methods, and some counted people whose returning symptoms may have had other explanations.

Researchers have also differed in what they count as tachyphylaxis. Some focus on depression returning after treatment initially helped. One study examined a particular group of symptoms, including tiredness, reduced motivation and difficulty thinking clearly.

But these symptoms do not, by themselves, show that a medicine has stopped working. They can be part of depression or occur as side-effects of treatment, so a doctor needs to assess what has changed before deciding how to respond.

What can be done if an antidepressant stops working?

The first step is to review what has changed. A doctor will usually ask about symptoms and how the medicine is being taken, including whether side-effects or difficulties getting prescriptions have led to missed doses. They may also consider other health conditions and medicines.

If treatment is no longer helping sufficiently, options can include adjusting the dose or switching antidepressants. A talking therapy may also help. This involves working with a trained therapist to understand and address difficulties affecting mental health.

Sometimes another medicine is added to the existing antidepressant. This requires discussion of the possible benefits and additional side-effects, and may involve specialist advice. A higher antidepressant dose is not always more effective and can increase side-effects.

However, there is limited evidence to show which approach works best specifically for antidepressant tachyphylaxis. Treatment therefore needs to reflect the person’s symptoms, previous experience and preferences.

Researchers still lack clear answers about why antidepressants appear to stop working for some people and how best to respond in those cases. Given how widely these medicines are used, these are substantial gaps in the evidence.

Anyone who feels that a previously helpful antidepressant is becoming less effective should discuss the change with their doctor. Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, including dizziness, anxiety and changes in mood, which can themselves feel like depression returning. Any change to treatment should be planned with the prescriber.

Colin Davidson has previously received funding from GSK, the NIH (USA) and the European Community for projects related to psychoactive drugs. He is currently a consultant on novel psychoactive substances for the UK Defence Science Technology Labs and is a member of the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs (UK).

articles.title: Misophonia: when everyday sounds become unbearable
articles.author: Mercedeh Erfanian, Research assistant professor, ESSCA School of Management
articles.summary: Noises that aren’t nerve-wracking for most people can trigger intense stress in people with misophonia.
articles.contentHtml:
KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • For people with misophonia, certain sounds trigger default reactions of aversion and anger.

  • Although it can be debilitating in everyday life, this condition is not simply a matter of heightened sensitivity to sounds.

  • Misophonia manifests as a wide range of symptoms and disorders affecting several areas, both emotional and cognitive.

Most people find some sounds unpleasant, such as a baby crying or a siren, because of features such as their pitch/frequency or loudness. However, for some people, very ordinary sounds, such as chewing, sniffing, breathing, swallowing, finger tapping or clicking a pen, can cause an immediate, intense reaction that is difficult to control, a condition known as misophonia.

A real medical condition

Misophonia is not simply being “annoyed by noise”. It is a real condition, usually described as a reduced tolerance to certain sounds or to things associated with those sounds. These sounds can cause very strong emotional, physical and behavioural fight or flight reactions that can result in the form of anger, disgust, anxiety, panic, muscle tension, increased heartbeat, an urge to leave the situation or stop the sound, and, more rarely, verbal or physical aggression.

In most cases, the loudness of the sound is not the main problem. The reaction depends more on the type of sound, what it means to the person, the situation in which it happens and sometimes even who is making it. For example, the sound of someone chewing may be unbearable when it comes from a particular person, like a husband, wife, mother or father, but much easier to tolerate in another situation.

People with misophonia often notice that their reactions happen automatically and are particularly intense and out of proportion. Misophonia can, therefore, have a major effect on everyday life. Eating with family, attending a class, working in a shared office, using public transport or maintaining close relationships can become very difficult. Some people also react strongly to visual cues linked to sounds, such as seeing someone chew or make repetitive movements, known as misokinesia.

Misophonia is frequently associated with various psychiatric disorders, including obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression and anxiety disorders. Interestingly, however, misophonia is not currently recognised as a separate disorder in the main international medical classification systems, and this remains an area of scientific debate.

Research into the causes

Researchers have been trying to understand misophonia for some years now. In hearing research, it has often been studied alongside other conditions involving reduced sound tolerance, such as hyperacusis and phonophobia. However, these conditions are different. Hyperacusis mainly involves being unusually sensitive to the loudness of sounds, which can sometimes cause pain. Phonophobia, by contrast, mainly involves fear of certain sounds.

Other researchers suggest that misophonia may involve an unusual connection between sounds and emotions. The brain hears the sound normally, but the emotional and physical response becomes much stronger than expected.

More recent research suggests that the condition is not simply about being sensitive to sounds. Trigger sounds are clearly important, but many people report that their reaction also depends on the situation, what they expect, how much control they feel they have, who is making the sound and what they believe the sound means. The same sound may be completely tolerable in one situation and unbearable in another. For example, many people with misophonia find it easier to tolerate a sound made by an animal or a young child than the same sound made by an adult, particularly someone close to them.

Is it linked to how well we adapt to situations and manage our emotions?

Our recent research explores this possibility. We studied whether misophonia is also linked to cognitive and emotional flexibility. Cognitive flexibility is the ability to change and adapt the way we think when a situation changes. Emotional flexibility is the ability to shift our attention or adjust our response when dealing with emotional information.

Our findings suggest that more severe misophonia may be linked to lower levels of both types of flexibility. In everyday life, this could mean that when a trigger sound occurs, it becomes harder to shift attention away from it, see the situation differently or return to a calmer emotional state. The reaction may then continue: the sound takes over the person’s attention, the emotional response becomes stronger, and it becomes difficult to move on from it, even when the person knows that the sound is harmless or was not made deliberately.

This difficulty may also help explain why some people continue to feel angry, tense or distressed even after the sound has stopped, or why they may keep thinking about the event for a long time afterwards. Misophonia may therefore not only involve strong sensitivity to certain sounds, but difficulty moving away from them mentally and emotionally.

Lower flexibility may also lead to stronger expectations about how other people should behave. As a result, behaviour that does not match these expectations may be more likely to cause a negative emotional reaction.

How we interpret other people’s behaviour plays a role in misophonia

Most trigger sounds are made by other people. The reaction may therefore depend not only on the sound itself, but also on how the other person’s behaviour is understood. Does the sound seem unnecessary, avoidable or deliberate? Is it seen as disrespectful?

This is why ideas such as theories involving mind and empathy may be important for future research. The mind is our ability to understand what other people may be thinking or intending while empathy is our ability to understand or share another person’s emotions.

Our future study will aim to understand these processes more clearly. This could help us move beyond overly simple explanations of misophonia as just being sensitive to noise or easily irritated. It may also improve public understanding, clinical assessment and support for people affected by misophonia.

For more information

If you think you might also display extreme sensitivity to sound and would like to find out more about related research and opportunities to take part in future studies, please contact: Mercedeh Erfanian

Most of the references cited in this article refer to my (peer-reviewed) scientific work, which focuses either on the soundscape, on auditory neuroscience, or more specifically on misophonia.

articles.title: The mental health of politicians is a critical issue – we should all care
articles.author: James Weinberg, Senior Lecturer in Political Science, University of Sheffield
articles.summary: Elected politicians make decisions that can affect millions, but do they receive the support they need?
articles.contentHtml:
When political leaders disclose mental health challenges, the public debate usually focuses on their personal experiences, resilience and even electoral prospects.

Meanwhile, a growing body of academic research has identified a range of stressors that impact politicians’ mental health. These include the organisational culture of parliaments, online harassment and abuse, job insecurity, inflated public expectations and a lack of control over policy outcomes.

Yet behind individual stories of mental ill-health in politics lies a far more consequential question for democracy. When elected representatives experience psychological distress, how does it alter the high-stakes choices they make on our behalf?

The existence of a relationship between our mental health and our capacity to operate well is not a mystery. Scientists have been researching this for decades. The unsurprising consensus is that poor psychological health does indeed impact our ability to process issues and make decisions.

Common mental health conditions, such as depression and anxiety, are known to introduce negative biases, distort perception of risk, and reduce openness to change. However, knowledge of how this works in politics – where decisions are required daily and on a scale that is likely to affect millions of lives – is limited.

Our recent publication provides the first empirical test of how symptoms of mental ill-health impact decision-making in office.

Analysing data from national politicians across two studies, we found that poor mental health does not simply make political life harder for politicians. It directly alters how they evaluate their own capability, assess risk and respond to information.

Doubting decisions under pressure

In our first study, we tracked 85 UK MPs over time using the General Health Questionnaire, an assessment to measure mental wellbeing, and a range of questions about decision-making capabilities.

Sitting MPs were invited to consider their thinking when voting, responding to debates, giving media interviews, and dealing with constituency requests. In other words, we asked about aspects of their job which are relatively high profile and central to their function in office.

Our questions pushed them to reflect on how frequently they experienced the limiting effects of time constraints, complex scenarios, daily challenges and positive or negative feedback from colleagues.

The results showed a negative link between prior experience of poor mental health and MPs’ perceptions of their own capability, especially when under time pressure.

Very simply, politicians with experience of poor mental health reported greater difficulty taking decisions quickly, coping with workplace interruptions and feeling as though they had sufficient time to deliberate.

Risk aversion

While self-evaluations offer insight into workplace confidence, how does mental ill-health affect actual policy choices or governing behaviour?

Our second study in our publication offers some insight into this question using data collected from 128 MPs in the UK, Canada and South Africa. We measured MPs’ depressive symptoms using the Patient Health Questionnaire, a standard clinical screening tool. We then placed them in hypothetical scenarios involving a public health emergency, a party polling discussion, and an economic policy vote.

Of the sampled parliamentarians, 12% met the clinical cut-off for major depression. We found higher rates among women, ethnic minorities, and younger representatives.

When faced with decision scenarios, politicians experiencing moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms were significantly less likely to take risky decisions in each situation compared to their peers. This was true even if that decision might have greater pay-offs for themselves, their party, or the public.

When scenarios were described around potential losses rather than gains, such as emphasising the impact on lives or votes, the same politicians were more susceptible to manipulation than their peers. This triggers an uptick in reactive decision-making.

These findings suggest that psychological distress alters the cognitive condition of our politicians in much the same way it does for the public.

Yet modern governance requires elected officials to tackle huge, complex problems, from climate change to economic strategy. These problems demand bold innovation, long-term trade-offs and being comfortable with uncertainty.

When psychological distress shifts politicians’ behaviour toward heightened risk aversion or shortcut thinking, the broader democratic process and outcomes of our politics are likely to suffer through constrained action.

Fix the institution before the individual

It should come as no surprise that symptoms of poor psychological health affect MPs as they might the rest of the population. The temptation to consider politicians as “others” who are not like us is in itself a risky assumption.

In most workplaces, allowances are made for time away from work or altered working practices to help support individuals through personal life events. Logically – and just as importantly – this should be the same in the political sphere.

Far from reinforcing an outdated response to political stress that demands greater personal toughness from our political leaders, we argue that our findings demand a fundamental shift in attitude and practice. The mental health of politicians must be treated as a major job issue, and of importance to our democratic process.

We suggest a number of necessary steps that might be tested or implemented by parliaments and political parties to safeguard individuals and outcomes. These include setting up dedicated occupational health systems and sources of psychological support within political parties.

Induction and training programmes for politicians in the UK Parliament and other legislatures also remain overly technical, procedural, and do not translate into ongoing support for a job that takes a sustained psychological toll. Continuing professional development opportunities, linked to job descriptions that make clear expectations of MPs, would be a good step in the right direction.

Ultimately, elected representatives are human beings operating in exceptionally demanding environments. Our focus on their mental health is not intended to undermine anyone’s potential to do the job, but rather to bolster calls for better support for MPs.

After all, ensuring our politicians are able to operate at their best is in all our interests. Protecting their mental health is not about granting them privilege. It is vital for ensuring sound, well-considered and resilient decisions for the public good.

James Weinberg receives funding from the Economic and Social Research Council.

Ashley Weinberg does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: One in three Ukrainian civilians estimated to meet the criteria for PTSD or complex PTSD – new study
articles.author: Gwendolyn Sasse, Einstein Professor for the Comparative Study of Democracy and Authoritarianism, Humboldt University…
articles.summary: War-related trauma now affects most people in Ukraine and presents a major threat to the country’s resiliance in the face of continuing Russian aggression.
articles.contentHtml:
Resilience is a word frequently used to describe the way Ukrainian society has responded to the war with Russia. It’s a term that can inspire sympathy and mobilise support. But it also risks overshadowing effects of war that require both domestic and international attention to enable Ukraine to withstand Russia’s invasion and manage long-term recovery.

The protracted conflict that started with Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, continued with the war in Donbas and escalated into Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 has recently reached a new level of intensity through concerted Russian attacks on civilian targets. As a result, the effects of war at the level of individuals, communities and society at large are becoming ever more apparent.

Trauma is an unavoidable effect of war. Measuring the psychological effects of trauma in countries following war and conflict can be difficult. Obtaining a reliable picture of the situation in Ukraine – where, after four and a half years, there is no end to the conflict in sight – has proved even more challenging.

The KonKoop Trauma Study, which has involved researchers from the Centre for East European and International Studies (ZOiS) in Berlin, King’s College London, the Kyiv School of Economics, George Washington University, the University of Manchester and the UK veteran mental health charity Combat Stress is, as far as we are aware, the first representative survey of the civilian population. This survey, implemented by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology, now provides a baseline measure of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and complex PTSD in Ukraine.

Standard PTSD often stems from a single event (such as a car crash or – as in Ukraine – a single violent episode connected to the ongoing conflict). It’s characterised by symptoms such as intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance of reminders of the trauma and feeling constantly on alert.

CPTSD, meanwhile, typically results from repeated or very severe (also referred to as complex) trauma, or both. It displays the same symptoms as PTSD, but also involves persistent difficulties with self-worth, emotional regulation and relationships.

In May 2024, we conducted a nationally representative survey of 2,504 adults living in government-controlled regions of Ukraine. Participants were randomly selected and interviewed by mobile phone allowing us to reach people from across the country, including displaced individuals. Mobile phone coverage in Ukraine stood at 96% in 2020.

This type of computer-assisted interviewing is the only means of direct survey access at this point and preferable to an online survey, but may have resulted in some selection bias (due to lack of access to those without phones or those in frontline combat roles) and possible underreporting of trauma exposure or post-traumatic symptoms, due to experiences of shame or stigma. The aim was not to systematically include military personnel.

We examined exposure to traumatic events across people’s lives, experiences directly related to the war, and symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD) as defined in the World Health Organization’s ICD-11 diagnostic system.

Our findings reveal the extraordinary scale of trauma Ukrainian civilians have been exposed to. This study systematically includes pre-war trauma in the analysis, as trauma can build over time. More than three-quarters of respondents reported experiencing at least one traumatic event during adulthood, while almost half reported traumatic experiences during childhood.

Many participants described experiences that have become commonplace during wartime. These included shelling and destruction in their neighbourhoods, losing loved ones and having family members forced to leave their homes. Importantly, trauma exposure was already high before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.

This reflects both the cumulative effects of a decade of war, as well as historical and intergenerational traumas that have shaped Ukrainian society. Our further research will try to explore how trauma inflicted during the war combines with and contrasts from pre-war trauma, something not yet clear from our work so far.

We estimated that 31.2% of adults met the criteria for either PTSD or CPTSD. Approximately one in four met the criteria for PTSD, while a smaller proportion, around 6%, met the criteria for CPTSD. Taken together, along with the fact that many Ukrainians will be suffering significant trauma-related symptoms that do not meet the threshold for these disorders, these figures suggest that trauma-related mental health difficulties represent a major public health challenge.

What the study discovered

Several factors were associated with a greater likelihood of developing PTSD or CPTSD. Women were more likely than men to meet diagnostic criteria. So were people who had been displaced by the war, those with lower educational attainment and those with a history of military service.

We also found a clear cumulative effect of trauma. The greater the number of traumatic experiences an individual had encountered in their lives, and the greater the number of harmful, unpleasant or frightening war-related incidents they had experienced, the higher their likelihood of meeting criteria for PTSD or CPTSD.

Violence from other people and life-threatening experiences showed the strongest links with PTSD and CPTSD. This is consistent with a large body of international trauma research.

One of the most striking findings of the study was the relatively low prevalence of CPTSD compared with PTSD, given the duration of the conflict in Ukraine and the frequently complex nature of traumas experienced. Previous studies conducted in other conflict settings have suggested that CPTSD may be as common as, or even more common than, PTSD.

In our research, however, suspected cases of PTSD were substantially more prevalent. While the reasons for this remain uncertain, several explanations are possible. CPTSD is generally associated with prolonged, repeated and inescapable traumatic experiences, particularly those involving being abused, coerced or held captive.

Many Ukrainians have undoubtedly been exposed to such experiences over the past decade. But the pattern of exposure in the wider Ukrainian population may differ from that seen in groups such as internally or externally displaced populations, such as in Gaza, where research has found that CPTSD accounts for anywhere from one-third to a full half of all trauma diagnoses.

It is also possible that social support networks, community solidarity and strong national identity have helped protect against some of the more enduring disturbances in self-worth and relationships that characterise CPTSD.

What this means for Ukraine

Our findings raise questions about how trauma should be understood in the context of an active war. Most models of PTSD assume that the traumatic event occurred in the past. In Ukraine, however, the threat remains current. The common symptoms of hypervigilance, anxiety and heightened alertness may not simply represent pathological reactions to past events. They may also reflect realistic responses to present dangers.

This perspective aligns with emerging theories of “continuous traumatic stress”, which first emerged from apartheid-era South Africa and have been explored in recent research in Ukraine. This would suggest that traditional post-traumatic frameworks may not fully capture psychological responses in settings where exposure to threat is ongoing and there is no clear endpoint to the trauma.

The findings highlight the urgent need for mental health support in Ukraine, including from international health providers. While access to evidence-based trauma therapies remains important, the sheer scale of need means that specialist services alone are unlikely to be sufficient.

Community-based interventions, peer support networks and programmes that strengthen social connectedness may play an equally important role. As the war continues, understanding how people adapt, cope and respond psychologically to ongoing threat will be crucial in shaping both mental health policy and Ukraine’s longer-term recovery.

The psychological impacts of war reach beyond the individual to Ukrainian society as a whole. They are bound to shape the continuing war effort. But they will also affect long-term social cohesion, behaviour, trust – and, possibly, political attitudes among the Ukrainian people.

The study was funded by the German Federal Ministry for Research, Space and Technology as part of the research network KonKoop (Conflict and Cooperation in Eastern Europe) led by the Centre for East European and International Studies (ZOiS). ZOiS receives institutional funding from the German Federal Foreign Ministry.

The study funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space. The collaboration involved researchers from King’s College London, the University of Manchester, Kyiv School of Economis and George Washington University. The survey was implemented by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology.
